KEY MESSAGE 1. Frost concerns for portions of the area later tonight 
into early Monday morning.

A narrow mid level ridge from the upper Ohio Valley to southern New 
England is forecast to weaken some tonight into Monday. Surface high 
pressure stretched southwest to northeast across our area will also 
weaken a bit through tonight. As this occurs, a closed low off the 
coast of the Carolinas will support surface low pressure also well 
off those coasts. This will start to tighten the pressure gradient 
northward into our area later tonight and Monday morning. This will 
have implications on the surface winds. Most inland areas should 
decouple for a while tonight, however areas closer to the coast 
(especially near and south/east of I-95) may have a northeasterly 
wind increase some overnight and especially Monday morning. Given 
the presence of the ridge aloft and surface high pressure directly 
over the interior areas longer, there is a greater risk of frost 
tonight and early Monday morning. Therefore, opted to issue a Frost 
Advisory for areas near and north/west of I-95 for where the growing 
season continues. For areas south and east of there, patchy frost is 
possible away from the coasts but with lower confidence on 
widespread frost opted to hold off on any frost advisories. 

After a chilly/cold start Monday, a milder afternoon is forecast 
with high temperatures topping out right near average away from the 
immediate coast. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...A nor'easter developing off the coast of the
southern Mid-Atlantic is expected to bring coastal impacts and 
create hazardous marine conditions through at least the middle 
of this week.

The base of a deep trough axis that is located just offshore
will cutoff into an upper level low tonight which will then meander
over the southern Mid- Atlantic coast over the next few days. 
At the same time, strong and expansive high pressure will be 
building over the Ohio Valley. As a result, a nor'easter is 
developing off the North Carolina coast and is expected to 
continue to strengthen and meander offshore into the middle of
this week.

Overall, confidence has increased that through at least
Wednesday, the nor'easter will remain close enough to bring
multiple impacts to our coastal areas. Persistently strong 
northeast winds will push water towards the coast. Multiple 
rounds of coastal flooding are likely (see key message 3 below).
Increasing seas may result in beach erosion in some areas as 
well. For areas along the immediate coast, gusty winds up to 
around 30-35 mph are possible.

Inland, impacts will be limited to none with how far offshore
the storm is likely to be. In fact, outside of a few showers at
the coast, little to no precipitation is likely at all over 
land areas.

For Thursday and beyond, there still remains more uncertainty in
the forecast. However, the prevailing consensus is trending 
towards the storm being swept out to sea which would likely 
result in an improvement in conditions along the coast. Notably,
though, there are still multiple members of both the EC and 
GEFS ensemble suites that have the nor'easter continue to linger
in our offshore waters towards the end of the week.

KEY MESSAGE 3...A prolonged period of onshore flow will lead to 
multiple elevated high tide cycles this week resulting in rounds of 
coastal flooding.

As the nor'easter develops and meanders offshore through at
least the middle of the week, there will be a persistent and 
strong northeast wind in place. This will lead to a prolonged 
period of onshore flow resulting in multiple elevated high tide 
cycles. The first high tide cycle of concern is currently 
expected to be Tuesday evening as spotty minor to minor tidal 
flooding is forecast. A Coastal Flood Advisory has been issued 
for the Tuesday evening high tide cycle for Ocean, southeastern 
Burlington, Atlantic, Cape May, Kent, and Sussex County 
Delaware. This Advisory goes from 3 PM to 9 PM Tuesday and is 
for widespread minor coastal flooding. 

The high tide cycle late Tuesday night into early Wednesday 
morning, looks to bring another round of spotty minor to
widespread minor tidal flooding. An additional Coastal Flood
Advisory will likely be needed for Ocean, southeastern Burlington, 
Atlantic, Cape May, Kent, and Sussex County Delaware.

Additional coastal flood hazards will likely be needed for high
tide cycles Wednesday, and potentially Thursday, as the high 
tide cycles remain elevated. From the current forecast, 
Wednesday evening's high tide cycle looks to be the one of most 
concern with widespread minor to low-end moderate coastal 
flooding. Beyond Wednesday evening, another round of coastal 
flooding is possible but uncertainty remains in the exact extent
as it will be dependent on the location of the nor'easter.
